newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia job market seen still weak.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia job market seen still weak.

text.p: Australian markets will receive a final reminder of the nation's stalling labour market in 1996 when employment figures for November are released on Thursday.
Employment has been one of the softest areas of the economy over 1996, and a key factor behind the decision of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to cut rates twice since July.

With little prospect of a sustained jobs recovery seen until around the middle of 1997, economists said the November data would likely support market expectations of a rate cut some time in the first quarter of 1997.
The median forecast fo the 28 economists surveyed by Reuters was for jobs growth of about 10,000 positions in November, with forecasts ranging from a fall of 15,000 to a rise of 40,000.

While employment growth is generally expected to rise, the November forecasts are for growth typical of what has been seen so far this year -- jobs growth not fast enough to make inroads into unemployment.
If the median forecast is met it will be the eighth month out of the 11 so far this year that employment has risen.

Despite this, employment levels will only be up 47,200 on where they were last December. This equates to average monthly growth in 1996 of around 4,300 jobs per month, compared with average monthly employment growth of around 22,600 in 1995.
Reflecting the weak employment growth, forecasts for the unemployment rate centre on 8.7 percent, compared with 8.8 percent in October.
The most pessimistic forecast has unemployment back at 9.0 percent, a level it has not been at since December 1994.

The combination of weak employment growth and continuing high unemployment has led to growing expectations that the RBA may have to cut interest rates for a third time, after reductions in July and November.
"We expect the tepid jobs growth story to have continued in November," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
"Such a result would buttress our view that the RBA will need to cut rates again in the coming months to further stimulate employment growth," Peters said.
When annoucing the second cut in interest rates last month, the RBA said monetary policy should not stand in the way of growth if it could be achieved without threatening inflation.
"In current circumstances, with employment growth moderate and with unemployment still relatively high, the scope for strong growth ought to be ample," the RBA said.
However, the rate cuts will have minimal short term impact on the unemployment rate, which may rise even higher in coming months, economists said.
"The weakness of the labour market seems set to persists for some time yet, probably until around mid-1997," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
The ANZ job advertisement series, a forward indicator of employment, rose in November after four months of falls.
However, ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said it would be premature to see the rise as a clear signal of an improving jobs market.
